units.explanation: The PR replaces a parameterized query with one that builds SQL text by string concatenation. In update_link_info, the url values from the `data` argument (x[3]) are joined with "','" and interpolated directly into an f-string passed to self.c.execute. These url values originate from user-supplied download links (info_thread -> update_file_info -> update_link_info), so an attacker can inject arbitrary SQL via a crafted url containing a single quote. The old code used placeholders ('?') with bound parameters; the new code does not bind or escape the values.

check_db_or_user_exists builds SQL by string-formatting db_name (and db_user) directly into the query text and executes it with cur.execute. These values originate from attacker-controlled request input: management_resources.py parses 'db_name' from the request (line 130) and passes it into the entity, which is then passed to PGClusterBackend.exists(entity) -> check_db_or_user_exists(entity.db_name, ...). Because the value is concatenated into the SQL string rather than bound as a parameter, an attacker can inject arbitrary SQL (e.g. a db_name containing a single quote) into the executed statement.

units.reason: gold section has no SQL signal; the pipeline would not send it to the SQLi reviewer

units.explanation: In QueryParser.parse (changed line 289), the attacker-controlled `default_field` value is spliced into the SQL text via `sql.replace('__default_field__', default_field)` with no allowlist or quoting. `default_field` originates from the `q.df` request parameter (alerta/database/backends/postgres/utils.py:150, `default_field=params.get('q.df')`), and the parser's `field_name` grammar (queryparser.py:244) accepts arbitrary words, so a value containing a single quote can break out of the `"__default_field__"` identifier and inject SQL. Unlike the other dynamic parts (which are now bound via `params`), this identifier is inserted as raw text.

The new `where_in` Jinja filter (superset/jinja_context.py:404-420) builds a SQL `IN (...)` clause by string-concatenating user-controllable values. It is registered as a template filter (line 456) and documented to be applied to `filter_values(...)` / `get_filters(...)` values (docs/docs/installation/sql-templating.mdx:209,248), which are attacker-influenced filter values. The only sanitization is `value.replace(mark, mark*2)` (line 415), a hand-written quoting helper that escapes only the single-quote character. This is insufficient: it does not escape backslashes (breaks MySQL/Postgres backslash-escape dialects), does not handle other quote styles, and non-string values are emitted via raw `str(value)` (line 417) with no escaping at all. The resulting text is interpolated directly into the SQL query, so a crafted filter value can break out of the quoted literal and inject arbitrary SQL.

The new `api_key` query parameter (attacker-controlled via the GET /global/spend/logs request) is concatenated directly into a raw SQL string and executed via prisma_client.db.query_raw. The value is placed between single quotes with no parameter binding, escaping, or allowlist, so an attacker can break out of the string literal (e.g. api_key=' OR '1'='1) to inject arbitrary SQL.

replace_query_parameters (newly added) builds SQL by string-replacing {{key}} placeholders with attacker-controlled parameter values (from parse_qs of the request params string) and returns the text, which get_query_results then passes to query.data_source.query_runner.run_query(query_text, user) for execution. The values are concatenated directly into the SQL text with no binding, escaping, or allowlist, so a parameter value can inject arbitrary SQL into the target data source's query.

The new PostgreSQL explain_query_prefix() builds the EXPLAIN prefix by string-concatenating the option names and the format value (prefix += ' (%s)' % ', '.join('%s %s' % i for i in extra.items())). The option names come from self.query.explain_options, which is set from the **options keyword arguments of QuerySet.explain() (query.py:522 q.explain_options = options) and passed through compiler.py:536 (**self.query.explain_options). These option NAMES are identifiers (e.g. ANALYZE, BUFFERS, COSTS) that are interpolated directly into the SQL text with no allowlist and no quoting/escaping. The base class only validates the format value against supported_explain_formats and rejects options entirely (base/operations.py:670-671), but the PostgreSQL override bypasses that by accepting arbitrary option names and embedding them verbatim. An attacker who can influence the explain() options (e.g. via a template/API argument or stored value) can inject arbitrary SQL into the EXPLAIN statement. The format value is allowlisted, but the option names are not.
